hero.title: School Support
hero.subtitle: Elmbrook School District backs GEarheads at every level — covering costs, opening up space, and clearing away the barriers that keep most robotics teams from growing.

impact.label: District Partnership
impact.text: GEarheads has real backing at three levels: the Elmbrook superintendent, the Brookfield Central principal, and the school's athletic director. That means budget decisions and scheduling requests have someone in the building who can say yes. Most FTC teams don't get that kind of buy-in — it's why we can offer things other teams have to pay for out of pocket.

stats.label: BCHS Club Fee
stats.hint: Annual student fee covering team operations

facets.question: How does the district partnership actually work?
facets.description: It's not a sponsorship — no check gets written. The district backs us at every level, and that's what does the real work. The superintendent calls the team a model for STEM access, so our requests carry weight. The principal handles practice space, storage, and hosting visiting teams. The athletic director treats FTC like a sports program, so we get athletics infrastructure and event support too. We're not renting space from a school — we're embedded in it. That's how we can host a 26-team tournament with overnight approval, not a six-week wait.

facets.question: What do FLL and FTC registration and field costs actually cover — and why does the district paying them matter?
facets.description: FIRST robotics isn't cheap — registration fees, a new field element kit every year, tournament entry fees. FLL runs similar costs. Without help, that's pay-to-play: only families who can spend a few hundred dollars a year get in. Elmbrook covers registration and field hardware in full for both programs at Brookfield Central, so no student gets turned away over cost. A student who starts in FLL in fifth grade and is still in FTC by ninth grade has had four or five seasons covered — that's what lets us recruit broadly, not just from families who can self-fund.

facets.question: How has school support increased physical robotics space over time?
facets.description: Space is the hardest thing for most high school robotics teams — shared rooms, no storage, nowhere to leave a half-built robot overnight. Ours has improved every season. Early on it was a shared classroom after hours; now we have dedicated storage for the robot, field elements, and tools, plus use of the gym floor, hallways, and the school's fabrication space for practice and hosting other teams. That scale is why we could host 26 FTC teams for the Rookie Qualifier — gym floor, judging rooms, a pit area, parking, all committed by the school.

facets.question: What is the ~$100 BCHS club fee model, and how does it fit into the broader cost picture?
facets.description: BCHS charges a standard club fee — about $100 a year — low enough for most families, covering team operations like tools, wiring, and filament, since the district already covers registration and field hardware. It also makes things official: students are enrolled in a real BCHS program, with liability coverage and a teacher supervisor attached. A competitive FTC season runs several thousand dollars once you count everything, so the $100 is a small piece — the rest comes from district subsidies, sponsors like GE HealthCare and Milliman, and fundraising. Families who can't pay get a hardship waiver.
